doc.title: Konitz Lee — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: The sound of the Thornhill band and Claude Thornhill as leader
summary: He recalls the ballad charts, the instrumentation, and Thornhill's quiet, non-committal leadership and piano touch.

story.theme_name: Leading a band: choosing, paying and managing players
story.community_name: Leading a band: running, choosing and keeping players

blocks.x: What was it like in general to play on that band, what was the feeling you got from it, especially from the ballad charts?

It was “goose pimply” sometimes it was so beautiful, with the two French horns and the Tuba to add. I can’t believe there were five [saxes]. There was a baritone player, I know, two Tenor players, I know.
On some for those records, there are as many as seven reeds.
That was before me, I think.
But definitely there were five when you were there?
How was Claude Thornhill as a leader and as a boss?

He was very non-committal. I think he just sat down and played, feed off the band every once in a while, but he was very quiet. I didn’t really hang out with him. He had a lovely wife that raveled with them. They kept apart pretty much, but he seemed always in good spirits. [He was] never too interested in stretching out or anything with whatever opportunity to play, just doing pretty much what was expected after I heard him the first time.
He wasn’t really a “jazz player” was he?

I think he had some of that experience, obviously, with different groups he had [or] had been part of. More, I guess, in the Teddy Wilson style or something like that, but never really developed to a high degree.
I’ve heard he was able to get the worst pianos, he encountered on the road, to sound good.
Yeah, I never remember them sounding bad, but very typical. Somehow, he put his stamp on it immediately.
